slides.name: The Power of AI
slides.notes:
THE POWER OF AI · ABOUT 40 MINUTES · FIVE QUESTIONS.

Let the title and the spoiler land. "Artificial intelligence" is a broad umbrella term, but public conversation has shrunk it to one narrow branch: generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot. The four stickers are the four kinds of AI we meet first; their colours stay the same all talk.

params.text: The Power of AI · Your speaker
Supporting AI literacy for over 1 million children across the country.
We’re encouraging businesses like yours to take part.

slides.notes:
YOUR SPEAKER · ABOUT 30 SECONDS. The QR code in the box opens the AI Awareness Day website, aiawarenessday.co.uk. Who you are, before any data: Mark Martin MBE, in education, R&D and computer science. Founder of AI Awareness Day, a nationwide campaign that builds AI literacy across schools; it supports over 1 million children across the country (its site says "we estimate we’re already reaching over 1,000,000 students").

Click for the ask. Next year’s AI Awareness Day is on Thursday 29 April 2027, and its theme is "Keep Humans in the Loop", the same message as this talk. This time it is asking businesses like the ones in this room to take part.

Then: "So, five questions."

slides.name: Five questions

params.text: How do I make it stick?

slides.notes:
One talk, five questions. Read them out; the label at the top of every slide says which one we are on.

01 What even is AI? (about 9 minutes). 02 Who’s actually using it? The UK numbers (about 8). 03 What happens to my job? A look inside the company that makes Claude (about 10). 04 Borrowed or owned? The idea the UKBT Institute is built on (about 6). 05 How do I make it stick? AI in your routine, without borrowing your skill: ten minutes a day from tomorrow, and the Institute’s method (about 7).

Bridge: "First question. When I say AI, what do you picture?"

slides.name: What people picture

params.text: Say “AI” and most people picture this:
↑ What you type here is called a prompt.
That’s one branch of AI. There are at least four.

slides.notes:
Ask the room: "When I say AI, what do you picture?" Most people picture a chat box.

Because business owners and the public have mostly met conversational chatbots, many SMEs assume "adopting AI" simply means typing prompts into a box. Point at the box: "What you type here is called a prompt." Say that assumption out loud. Think that, and you miss the wider toolkit that does the real work: the forecasting, the document reading, the routing, the agents.

Click: that is one branch. Over the next few slides we meet the other three, and why the difference matters for a business.

slides.name: AI is an umbrella

params.text: Four kinds sit under it. You’ve met one.

slides.notes:
Four kinds, one click each. Give each its nickname as it lands.

01 Generative: the public face. 02 Predictive and analytical: the quiet workhorse. 03 Automation and workflow: the efficiency engine. 04 Autonomous agents: the new frontier.

On the last click, ask the room: "Hands up for each kind you’ve used. One hand for one, two for two…"

Keep the colours in mind: they stay the same for the rest of the talk.

slides.name: Generative AI

params.text: Creates new text, images, code or audio, on demand.
Easy and impressive, so it owns the headlines. It can make things up (hallucinate), so a person checks its work.

slides.notes: 01 · GENERATIVE AI, THE PUBLIC FACE. Tools that create new text, images, code or audio on demand. They are accessible and impressive, which is why they dominate the headlines. They are also prone to hallucinations and need constant human supervision.

slides.name: Predictive & analytical AI

params.text: Software that learns patterns from your past data.
Quietly, inside the accounting, customer records and stock software you may already use.

slides.notes: 02 · PREDICTIVE AND ANALYTICAL AI, THE QUIET WORKHORSE. Machine-learning models that spot patterns in historical data: forecasting cash flow, predicting stock demand, flagging late-paying invoices, identifying customer churn (customers about to leave). These tools run quietly inside existing accounting, CRM and inventory software.

slides.name: Automation & workflow AI

params.text: Does the routine work, with nobody typing a prompt.
It works in the background of the job, not in a chat window.

slides.notes: 03 · AUTOMATION AND WORKFLOW AI, THE EFFICIENCY ENGINE. Systems that extract data from PDFs, read invoices, route customer support tickets, or transcribe and summarise meetings, without anyone prompting them.

slides.name: Autonomous AI agents

params.text: Goal-driven systems that plan multi-step tasks, use software tools and carry out workflows on their own.
Anthropic has measured the shift in its own company. We’ll look inside later.

slides.notes:
04 · AUTONOMOUS AI AGENTS, THE NEW FRONTIER. Goal-driven systems that can plan multi-step tasks, use software tools and execute workflows independently.

This is the shift examined in Anthropic’s "How employment is changing at Anthropic" (16 October 2026), the third question of the talk. Keep its numbers for then: don’t give them away here.

slides.name: Why the mix-up costs you

params.text: Chatbots are bad at exact sums, forecasts and strict look-ups. Force them and the errors pile up.
AI you pay for but never switched on
Accounting, customer records and shop software often has AI built in. It sits unused because “AI” sounds like a new licence.
A chatbot fluffing a blog post is low stakes. AI deciding about a customer brings UK GDPR duties.

slides.notes:
Three reasons, one click each.

1. Using the wrong tool for the job: when a firm thinks AI equals a chatbot, staff force large language models to do tasks they are bad at, such as deterministic accounting, stock forecasting or strict database look-ups. Frustration and errors follow.

2. Overlooking built-in tools: many UK SMEs already pay for predictive or automation AI inside platforms such as Xero, Sage, HubSpot or Shopify without switching those features on, because they assume AI means buying a separate chatbot licence.

3. Misjudging risk and governance: a chatbot hallucinating a marketing blog post is low risk; an autonomous agent or a predictive credit-scoring model making decisions on customer data carries serious UK GDPR and compliance implications.

The legal hook, if asked: under the UK GDPR, people have rights around significant decisions made about them by automated means, including the right to have a person review them. The ICO’s guidance on AI and data protection covers it.

factCheck.note: Card 2: that many UK SMEs pay for unused AI features in platforms such as Xero, Sage, HubSpot or Shopify. Find a source before saying it as a finding.

slides.name: Which AI is it?

params.text: Pull the totals off a pile of supplier invoices
Handle a refund start to finish, with a human for anything odd
Spot the customers about to leave
Transcribe and summarise the team meeting

slides.notes:
A quick-fire round. Read each task, let the room shout the kind, then click to show the answer sticker.

1 Forecast cash flow: predictive. 2 Pull totals off supplier invoices: automation and workflow. 3 Critique a draft: generative. 4 Handle a refund end to end with a human for exceptions: an agent. 5 Spot customers about to leave: predictive. 6 Transcribe and summarise a meeting: automation. If someone shouts "generative" for the summary, they have a point: the summary is usually written by generative AI inside the meeting tool. Use it: the kinds overlap, and the skill is matching the tool to the task.

The chatbot habit against the right AI, if you want an example per answer:
- Forecasting cash flow or sales: not pasting spreadsheets into a chatbot to guess next quarter, but the predictive AI built into accounting or ERP tools, modelling historical trends.
- Processing supplier invoices: not copying invoice text into a prompt one by one, but document and workflow AI (OCR plus automated rules) extracting and matching the data.
- Writing and brainstorming: not blindly handing over final client proposals, but generative AI as a sparring partner to critique drafts and test ideas.
- Multi-step customer support: not an unsupervised chatbot making refund promises, but an agent with strict standing instructions and a human for exceptions.

Land it: only one of the six is a chatbot job. AI is not a chatbot. It is a toolkit, and the skill is matching the type of intelligence to the job.

Bridge: "AI is a toolkit, not a chatbot. So who’s actually using the toolkit? Five big UK reports landed this year."

slides.name: It doubled in a year

params.text: of UK businesses used at least one AI tool in 2026
Source: DSIT, AI adoption survey 2026 (29 October 2026) · 3,503 businesses, January to April 2026

slides.notes:
SECOND QUESTION · WHO’S ACTUALLY USING IT? · ABOUT 8 MINUTES. Five major UK reports on small-business AI landed in 2026: the government (DSIT), the statisticians (ONS), a bank (NatWest), the chambers (BCC) and the small-business federation (FSB). Use roughly doubled in a year, but there is a sharp divide between trying the tools and changing how the business works.

Ask first, then let the number land: "Hands up if your business uses at least one AI tool."

DSIT, "AI adoption survey 2026" (29 October 2026): 3,503 telephone interviews between 7 January and 21 April 2026, plus 50 in-depth interviews and 7 site visits. 32% of UK businesses used at least one AI technology, against 16% in 2025. Larger firms: 52%.

Not on the slide: a breakdown of 27% micro, 34% small and 47% medium is quoted in coverage, but it is not in DSIT’s executive summary. Check the full report before quoting it.

slides.name: Depends who you ask

params.text: DSIT: the government · ONS: national statistics · NatWest: a bank · BCC: chambers of commerce · FSB: small-business federation
A third to a half of firms, depending on who’s counting, and how.

slides.notes:
Five surveys, five numbers, and they are not contradicting each other: each asks a different question of different firms. Say the range, not one figure.

DSIT 32% of UK businesses used at least one AI technology (October 2026). ONS about 35% of businesses with 10 or more staff (June 2026). NatWest 44% of firms use AI (September 2026). BCC 54% of firms actively using AI, 94% of them SMEs (March 2026). FSB 55% of small firms, up from 20% in 2023 (July 2026; from press reports of the FSB’s "The Confidence Code").

factCheck.note: The FSB figure (55%) comes from press reports of “The Confidence Code” (July 2026); the FSB report itself was not opened. Check it before the day.

slides.name: Bigger firms are further ahead
slides.notes:
Ask: "Hands up if you have fewer than ten staff." The smallest firms are furthest behind, and that is most of this room.

ONS, "Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026" (20 July 2026, BICS wave 159, fieldwork 5 to 28 June 2026): 28% of firms with 0 to 9 employees use AI, against 49% of those with 250 or more.

NatWest Group, AI growth gap research (25 September 2026, 1,400 UK SMEs and mid-market firms): 36% of smaller firms use AI, against 67% of those with more than 100 staff. NatWest does not state the cut-off for "smaller".

And by sector, in one line: ONS (20 July 2026, firms with 10 or more staff) finds adoption highest in information and communication, where almost three-fifths (58%) use AI, and as low as 13% in construction, about one in eight. The ONS article does not call construction the lowest of all industries, so do not say it is.

slides.name: Mostly admin and marketing

params.text: Of firms using, or planning to use, AI
77% use large language models: the chat tools from the start of the talk.
Source: DSIT, AI adoption survey 2026 (29 October 2026)

slides.notes:
DSIT (October 2026), among businesses using or planning to use AI: administration 81%, marketing 71%, IT 66%. Use is concentrated in natural language processing and text generation; large language models account for 77% of users or planned users.

The link back to the four kinds: most firms are using the public face of AI, generative chat tools, for admin and marketing. The other three kinds are mostly untouched.

slides.name: It’s helping. It’s worrying.

params.text: It’s helping. It’s worrying. It isn’t replacing people.
of small firms using AI say it has improved productivity
worry about the risks: data, copyright and liability
of SMEs using AI say their headcount hasn’t changed
Sources: FSB, The Confidence Code (July 2026), from press reports · BCC, Future of Work: AI in the Workplace (March 2026)

slides.notes:
Three numbers, one per click. Ask on the second: "Hands up if data, copyright or liability worries you."

FSB, "The Confidence Code: The Challenges and Opportunities of AI for Small Firms" (July 2026), as reported in the trade press: AI use among small firms has risen to 55%, from 20% in 2023; 59% of users say it has improved their productivity; 92% worry about the risks, with fears around data, liability and copyright holding many back. FSB estimates wider and deeper adoption could add more than £42 billion a year to the UK economy; that is a projection built on assumptions, so say it as one. Not on the slide: a 24% revenue-growth figure is quoted in some coverage but could not be confirmed.

British Chambers of Commerce with Atos, analysis by ISER/MiSoC at the University of Essex, "Future of Work: AI in the Workplace" (19 March 2026; 668 firms, 94% SMEs): 54% actively use AI; 95% of SMEs using AI report no change to workforce size over the past year; 86% say job roles are unchanged. About one in ten has gone further, into AI built for their business.

ONS (20 July 2026): of businesses citing a lack of AI expertise, around 62% train or retrain existing staff, against around 26% of businesses reporting no barriers. Train, don’t just hire.

So far, small firms are using AI to back their people, not to replace them.

Land the UK picture here (Wide, not deep is hidden): everyone’s trying it, almost nobody’s transformed. Trying AI is now normal, a third to a half of firms; changing how the business works with it is rare, about one in twenty (NatWest). That gap is the opportunity.

Bridge, which also squares the 95% with what comes next: "In small firms today, jobs haven’t gone. At the frontier, the shape of jobs is changing. Here’s a glimpse, inside the company that makes Claude."

factCheck.note: The FSB figures (59%, 92% and the £42bn projection) come from press reports of “The Confidence Code” (July 2026); the FSB report itself was not opened. Check them before the day.

slides.name: Wide, not deep

params.text: of firms have reached “transforming”: AI built into how they work.
Source: NatWest Group, AI growth gap research (25 September 2026) · 1,400 UK SMEs and mid-market firms

slides.notes:
NatWest Group (25 September 2026): 44% of businesses use AI, but 29% of those using it are still in the earliest piloting and awareness stages, saving 1 to 10% of working time. Only 6% have reached the transforming stage, where savings average 61 to 70%. NatWest’s own release is unclear whether the 6% is of all firms or of users, so say "about one in twenty". The barriers it names: skills, cost, uncertainty over which tools to use, in-house expertise, and security.

One click lights the six dots.

Land the UK picture here: everyone’s trying it, almost nobody’s transformed. Trying AI is now normal, a third to a half of firms; changing how the business works with it is rare, about one in twenty. Surface use, not deep: most firms use chat tools for admin and marketing (DSIT, NatWest), not new ways of working. That gap is the opportunity.

Bridge, which also squares the 95% with what comes next: "In small firms today, jobs haven’t gone. At the frontier, the shape of jobs is changing. Here’s a glimpse, inside the company that makes Claude."

slides.name: Why look at an AI company?

params.text: 3 of 5 · What happens to my job?
Why look at an AI company?
Jobs in small firms haven’t gone. Where agents arrive first, their shape is changing. A glimpse, not a forecast.
How employment is changing at Anthropic

slides.notes:
THIRD QUESTION · WHAT HAPPENS TO MY JOB? · ABOUT 10 MINUTES. The question everyone in the room has: what happens to my job, and my team’s? Most small firms are only starting with AI, and their jobs haven’t gone: 95% say headcount hasn’t changed (BCC). What changes first, at the frontier, is the shape of the work. One company is years ahead, because it makes the tools: Anthropic studied what happened inside it as AI agents spread. That is our look over the horizon.

Anthropic, "How employment is changing at Anthropic" (Wilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff and McCrory, 16 October 2026). It drew on hiring records, output measures, surveys, communications, calendars and 17 employee interviews.

Say why it matters: this is a company where AI agents are already part of everyone’s day, so it shows what a workplace looks like when they scale. It is not typical, and the authors say so (we come back to their caveats before the lessons).

slides.name: Six agent hours for every human hour

params.text: 3 of 5 · What happens to my job?
Six agent hours for every human hour.
Agent hours: time the AI spent working on tasks by itself.
By August 2026, staff’s own AI agents logged six hours of work for every hour their people worked.
Agent hours first passed human hours in March 2026. That’s hours of activity, not business value.
Source: Anthropic, How employment is changing at Anthropic (16 October 2026)

slides.notes:
The headline number: across the company, agent hours first passed human hours in March 2026; by August, staff’s own agents were logging about six hours for every hour their human handlers worked.

Say what it measures: hours of activity, not business value. The authors are careful about that, and so should we be.

Agent hours, plainly: time the AI spent working on tasks by itself.

For you: these are engineers, but the room works in admin and marketing. Picture an assistant drafting your emails, quotes and posts by itself all week. That is what agent hours are.

slides.name: Most of the time, the agent is waiting

params.text: 3 of 5 · What happens to my job?
Most of the time, the agent is waiting for you.
of every stretch of work with an agent, spent waiting for a person
“…every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention.”
An Anthropic employee, on running several agents at once: like babysitting.
Source: Anthropic, How employment is changing at Anthropic (16 October 2026)

slides.notes:
The bottleneck has moved. Around 80% of a Claude session is spent idly waiting for human input: review, clarification, approval. And for non-technical groups, reading all the output their interactive sessions produce would take over half the work week (the authors’ estimate, from text volume and an assumed reading speed of 250 words a minute).

Click: how it feels. Staff running several agents in parallel described a stream of notifications and approval requests; one compared it to babysitting, where every child "brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention". Others described themselves as "bottlenecking the agents": the slow part, holding the agents up.

Ask the room: "Who here already feels like the bottleneck for their own team?"

For you: it’s the AI-drafted quotes, replies and posts sitting in a queue, waiting for your yes.

The point for the room: agents don’t remove the work. They move it, from doing to checking.

slides.name: More output, and a new job

params.text: 3 of 5 · What happens to my job?
More output. And a new job: managing it.
pieces of finished work saved per engineer, against six months before
And undone later no more often than work people did by hand.
Writing rules for the AI, building checks, reviewing the output.
of the average person’s work sessions with AI

8,500 written rules the AI follows every time,
up from a few hundred a year before
Source: Anthropic, How employment is changing at Anthropic (16 October 2026)

slides.notes:
Output went up sharply. Each engineer saved about five times as many code commits (saved code changes) as six months earlier. Comparing 192 engineers who adopted coding agents with 74 who did not, agent-written code was no more likely to be deleted or rolled back later. Other teams (data scientists, lawyers, accounts payable, sales) also rose, but the report gives no multiples for them, so neither do we. The authors’ own warning, on the sticker in plain words: more code is not necessarily better code, and AI errors may be harder to spot.

Click: the new job. When reviewing raw output is exhausting, people build the system instead. "Meta-work" (managing the AI: writing standing instructions, written rules for the agents, monitoring, reviewing output) rose from 10% of the average employee’s AI sessions in autumn 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Standing instructions grew from a few hundred in July 2025 to 8,500 a year later.

The bars are drawn to scale against a third of all sessions, so 22% is just over twice 10%, as it should be.

For you: five times the drafts is five times the checking. Meta-work is your brand guide, your email templates, the checklist you write once for the AI to follow every time.

Source: Anthropic, How employment is changing at Anthropic (16 October 2026)

slides.notes:
The junior share of technical hires fell from 27% to 9%, and the junior share of technical staff from 21% to 14% since early 2025, while the company tripled in size. So the share falling does not by itself mean fewer juniors. Junior postings fell sharply after December 2025, and administrative hiring has not grown with the company, which the authors call "clerical-light".

In hiring managers’ interview notes, mentions of a candidate’s AI tool use tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical roles between 2024 and 2026 (from about 5% and 7% of assessments). These are interview notes, not job adverts. What it signals: judgement, autonomy and directing AI matter more; narrow manual execution matters less.

The columns are drawn to scale, from zero to 30%: grey is early 2025, orange is the share by the October 2026 report.

For you: think of the routine admin and marketing tasks a junior used to learn the job on. If AI does them, how does your next junior learn?

Turn to your neighbour, 30 seconds: "Which entry-level job in your firm changes first?"

slides.name: Read it with care

params.text: 3 of 5 · What happens to my job?
Much of what happens there can’t be copied across the economy.
More code, more agent hours: not the same as better work.
AI mistakes may be harder to spot, so quality checks can miss them.
The company grew fast at the same time, which explains some of the gain.

slides.notes:
Be the honest one in the room. These are the authors’ own caveats: Anthropic is unusual, and many of its practices cannot be replicated across the economy; more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact; AI errors may be harder to spot than human ones; business growth at the same time may explain some of the gains; employees chose when to adopt the tools; and the hours figures rest on assumptions (40-hour weeks, 250 words read a minute).

If asked about outside critics: commentators have pointed out that high activity is not the same as value if tired reviewers rubber-stamp the work. That is the next slide’s first lesson.

slides.name: What it means for your team

params.text: 3 of 5 · What happens to my job?
What it means for your team

layers.name: Icon disc · Checking becomes the bottleneck

params.text: Batch approvals and automate the routine checks, or seniors drown in review queues.
A flooded, tired reviewer waves subtle errors through. Check less, but check properly.

layers.name: Icon disc · Rethink the first job

params.text: Routine entry-level work is shrinking. Hire for judgement and problem framing, and keep growing juniors.

layers.name: Icon disc · Write the rules once

params.text: Prompt templates, brand rules and checklists, not one message at a time.

slides.notes:
What a small team takes from Anthropic’s report: an early warning not to confuse agent activity with productivity.

Your bottleneck shifts from doing to checking: deploying agents will not cure a small team’s workload if every output needs a manual sign-off; batch the approvals and automate the routine quality checks.

Protect against rubber-stamp risk: a lean team flooded with AI-made proposals, financial models or code gets review fatigue fast, and tired people approve subtle errors.

Rethink entry-level roles: routine execution work is shrinking, so future hires need judgement and problem-framing skills to direct the tools. Small firms still need to grow their own people, because the checker of tomorrow is today’s junior.

Invest in guardrails, "meta-work": Anthropic’s staff answered the surge with standing instructions and automated checks; for an SME that means reusable prompt templates, brand guardrails and checklists, not managing AI one message at a time.

Two more from the UK numbers, if there is time. Shadow AI: staff on personal AI accounts nobody approved, with nobody checking the work, which brings the same checking risks. Say this as what we see in firms: DSIT’s published summary does not measure it. Train, don’t just hire: around 62% of firms short of AI expertise train their own staff (ONS), so build judgement and AI supervision in the people you have.

slides.name: Your job moves

params.text: So, what happens to my job?

Your job doesn’t disappear.
It moves.
From doing the work to directing it, and checking it.
Checking takes the skill to spot its mistakes. That’s the skill AI can quietly erode.

slides.notes:
The answer to the third question. Land it, then pause: AI is more than a chatbot; most firms are trying it but few have changed how they work; and where agents arrive first, the work moves from doing to directing and checking. The skill to protect, in yourself and your team, is judgement.

Click, the bridge the whole talk turns on: "If your job becomes checking the AI’s work, you need the skill to spot its mistakes. And that’s exactly the skill AI can quietly erode." Then: "That’s the idea the UKBT Institute is built on."

slides.name: Borrowed, not owned

params.text: Output and skill can move in opposite directions. So we measure both.

slides.notes:
FOURTH QUESTION · BORROWED OR OWNED? · ABOUT 6 MINUTES. The idea the UKBT Institute is built on: what happens to people’s own skill as they lean on AI. Productivity and independence are the theory; the next few slides show it is grounded in evidence, pedagogy and measured impact.

The core claim, in the talk’s two words. Fast with AI is borrowed: if you can only do the task with AI, the skill is the AI’s. Good without it is owned: if you can still do it without AI, the skill is yours. Click for the second line. (The Institute’s own wording is "AI productivity without independence is borrowed, not owned"; on the slide it is said plainly, with each colour on its own meaning: orange for borrowed, green for owned, as on the map.) Speed and skill can move in opposite directions, so the Institute measures both, not just speed.

slides.name: Faster with it. Worse without it.

params.text: Better with it. Worse without it.
better grades than students without AI
Students on the plain version did worse than students who never had it.
The tutor, set up to give hints, not answers, largely removed the harm.
Most plain-version students just asked it for the answer.
Source: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS (2025) · about 1,000 high-school maths students

slides.notes:
Before the click, a vote: "Hands up if you think the students on the plain version did better once AI was taken away. Now worse?" Then click.

On the slide, "a ChatGPT-style tool" is the study’s GPT-4, in an interface made to work like ChatGPT. The "plain version" is its GPT Base, and the "hints-only tutor" is its GPT Tutor, set up to give hints, not answers.

Hamsa Bastani and colleagues (Wharton), "Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics", PNAS 122(26), 2025: nearly a thousand high-school maths students. With GPT-4 during practice, grades rose 48% with a plain ChatGPT-style tool ("GPT Base") and 127% with a tutor designed to safeguard learning ("GPT Tutor"), against students without AI. When access was taken away for the exam, the plain-GPT students did worse than students who never had it (17% worse, in the preprint); the tutor students did about as well as those who never had it. The chat logs showed most plain-GPT students simply asked for the answer.

The bars are drawn to scale against each other.

factCheck.note: The size of the exam drop (17%) is the preprint’s figure; check the published PNAS version before saying a number.

slides.name: The mirage feels like progress

params.text: Anthropic’s trial · developers learning a new coding tool
It feels easier. That’s the trap.
People using AI found the task easier.
points on a test of what they’d learned, afterwards: 50% against 67%.
The group without AI was the one that said it learned more.
Its authors expect the loss to be even greater with agent-style tools.
Source: Shen and Tamkin, How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills, Anthropic (January 2026) · 52 developers

slides.notes:
Why this is dangerous: it feels fine from the inside. Before the last click, a vote: "Which group said it learned more: with AI, or without?"

In Anthropic’s skill trial (Shen and Tamkin, January 2026, 52 mostly junior developers learning a new library), people with the AI assistant found the task easier, then scored 50% on the quiz against 67% for those coding by hand. Both groups enjoyed the task, and it was the group without AI that reported learning more.

Note: some summaries say the AI users felt they learned more. The paper says the opposite ("The control group (No AI) reported higher self-reported learning", section 5.2.2), so say it this way.

The last line links the agents back to this: the authors write that "the loss in knowledge is likely even greater in an agentic or autocomplete setting where composing queries is not required" (section 6.1), and that "accomplishing a task with new knowledge or skills does not necessarily lead to the same productive gains" (section 7). It is their expectation, not a finding. Your own gloss, said as yours, not theirs: with agents, you don’t even have to ask. And your advice from it: agents are fine for the craft you’ve already mastered, and risky for the one you’re still learning.

Both cards were checked in the paper (section 5.2.2): "participants in the treatment group (AI Assistance) found the task easier than the control group", and "The control group (No AI) reported higher self-reported learning".

slides.notes:
The model that anchors everything, in two words: owned and borrowed. Across: speed with AI. Up: your own skill, what you can still do without it.

Owned (top right) is the goal: fast, and still good without it. Borrowed (bottom right) is the danger, because it looks like success: fast, but lost without it. That is the mirage, and it is what the last two slides showed: the students on the plain version, and the developers who found the task easier. Click: most AI training pushes people right, towards speed, so the arrow runs from Stuck straight into Borrowed. Click: the Institute’s job is to move them up and right, into Owned.

Bridge: "Knowing the trap isn’t enough. Here’s why most people stall, and how to make it stick: AI in your routine, without borrowing your skill."

slides.name: Why people stall

params.text: 5 of 5 · How do I make it stick?
An illustration of how learning feels, not data from a study

layers.name: Thought · No idea what I’m doing. But I keep going.

params.text: No idea what I’m doing. But I keep going.

slides.notes:
FIFTH QUESTION · HOW DO I MAKE IT STICK? · ABOUT 7 MINUTES. Say what "it" is: make AI part of your routine, without borrowing your skill.

Learning a new tool is not a straight line up, and this is why so many firms stall (NatWest found 29% of firms using AI still in the earliest piloting stage).

Walk the curve, a click at a time. "Looks like fun": the first quick wins. "This is hard!": the first dip. "No idea what I’m doing, but I keep going": the climb. "Now I get it!" ... "or not": the novelty wears off right as the real work begins. "I know nothing!": the low point, where most people quit. Then "This actually makes sense", "Did I do that?", and "I did it!".

The curve is an illustration of how learning feels, not data from a study, and the slide says so. The point: the low point is normal, and it comes before fluency, not instead of it. The usual explanation is the brain’s novelty reward (the buzz of a quick win) fading once the tool feels familiar; that is popular psychology, so offer it as a way of thinking, not as a research finding.

Four reasons the buzz wears off, if you want them. The novelty cliff: exploring new features gives easy rewards; once the interface feels familiar, that reward stops. The competency dip: learning the basics feels fast, mastering the complex edge cases feels slow, and the gap between knowing how a tool works and being fluent with it causes frustration. Setup feels like progress ("tool-shifting procrastination"): setting up a new app or workflow feels like productive work; once it is done, you have to face the actual, often harder task the tool was meant to solve. Too many settings (decision fatigue): new tools come with endless customisation; spending energy tweaking settings drains the willpower needed for real work.

Ask the room: "Hands up if you’ve spent longer setting up a tool than using it."

slides.name: Push past the slump

params.text: 5 of 5 · How do I make it stick?
Skip the tutorials. Finish one small task that matters.
Time-limit the settings. Use a basic setup, as it is, for two weeks.
Keep it open, so starting is easy. Keep the thinking hard.
Small daily reps, not big breakthroughs.

slides.notes:
That low point on the curve: here is how to get past it, starting this week.

01 Build one real output: stop watching tutorials and use the tool to finish one small, meaningful task. A real result replaces the lost novelty with real progress.

02 Cap the tinkering: set a strict time limit for themes, plug-ins and settings; lock in a basic setup and use it as it is for two weeks.

03 Lower the friction: keep the tool open or pinned to your workspace, so starting takes no effort and habit does the work, not willpower. Make starting easy, but keep the thinking hard: the struggle is what makes the skill stick, so the ease is in opening the tool, not in handing it the thinking.

04 Ten minutes a day: use the tool for ten minutes a day rather than aiming for big breakthroughs. Small daily reps bridge the gap. The next slide gives the ten minutes a shape that keeps the skill owned.

slides.name: Ten minutes a day

params.text: 5 of 5 · How do I make it stick?
Two weeks. One tool. One real task. Every day:
Day 14: it’s starting to feel normal.

slides.notes:
The streak. One click fills the fortnight, a day at a time.

The ten minutes have a shape, on the stickers: try it yourself first, then ask the AI why, then check its answer. That keeps the skill owned, not borrowed. It is three of the Institute’s strands (try it yourself first, ask why, test without the AI), which the next slide shows.

Ask the room to commit now: "Pick one tool, one real task, and your ten minutes: try it, ask why, check it. Tell your neighbour when tomorrow you’ll do it."

Why "starting to feel normal", not "it’s just how you work": in Lally and colleagues’ habit study (European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010), a new habit took 66 days on average to become automatic, anywhere from 18 to 254. Two weeks is a start, not the finish.

Then the Institute’s method: "That habit is free. Making it stick across a whole team, without borrowing anyone’s skill, is what our method is for."

factCheck.note: Notes: Lally et al. (2010), 66 days on average to become automatic, from 18 to 254. Written from memory; check the paper before quoting the numbers.

slides.name: Eight strands, three pillars

params.text: 5 of 5 · How do I make it stick?
The evidence is early, and mostly short-term: a model we’re testing and refining.

slides.notes:
THE UKBT INSTITUTE’S METHOD. Bridge in, from the streak: "That habit is free. Making it stick across a whole team, without borrowing anyone’s skill, is what our method is for."

At the centre, the goal: owned, fast and still good without AI. Round it, eight strands, each pairing evidence, a teaching practice and a measure. The slide gives each in plain words, with the technical name under it.

01 Know where you start (Baseline before tools; prior knowledge). Evidence: Nobody was immune: without AI, people scored higher at every level of experience (Anthropic). We measure: An audit score before training.
02 Try it yourself first (Effortful practice; active learning). Evidence: Bjork’s desirable difficulties: struggle makes skills stick. We measure: The task done with and without AI.
03 Ask why, not just what (Engaged use, not delegation; engagement). Evidence: Conceptual questioners scored 65%+; delegators under 40% (Anthropic). We measure: How people use AI in real work.
04 Test without the AI (AI-off checks; formative assessment). Evidence: Wharton: the dependency only showed once AI was removed. We measure: Performance unplugged, over time.
05 Know when to doubt it (Calibrated trust; metacognition). Evidence: Trust in AI went with less critical thinking; self-confidence with more (CHI 2025). We measure: Errors caught in AI output.
06 Pick tools that teach (Guardrailed tools; instructional design). Evidence: Wharton: a tutor built to protect learning largely removed the harm. We measure: Tool stress-test ratings.
07 Learn together (Peer learning and safety; collaboration, belonging). Evidence: Self-determination theory: autonomy, competence and connection sustain motivation. We measure: Shared practices and adoption.
08 Measure speed and skill (Dual-metric impact; data-informed). Evidence: Productivity and learning can move in opposite directions. We measure: Speed and skill without AI, before and after.

Strand 01’s evidence, said carefully: Anthropic’s trial found the group without AI scored higher at every level of prior coding experience, so experience did not make anyone immune. (Some summaries say experienced developers were more resilient; the paper does not test that.) Strand 05 is Lee et al., Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon, CHI 2025: higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking, higher self-confidence with more. Strand 07 is Deci and Ryan’s self-determination theory, a theory of motivation rather than an AI study.

Click: the three pillars, the outer ring of the original wheel (they replace "digitally-enabled" there). Backed by research (evidence-based): we only teach what research supports. Built on how people learn (pedagogy-driven): training designed around how adults actually build skill, not around tool features. We prove it worked (impact-measured): every engagement reports speed and skill without AI, before and after. The last is the commercial edge: measuring dependence, not just speed, which the Institute’s audit already does.

Last click, the honest note. Say it plainly, because it is what makes the rest credible: the studies behind the strands are small and short-term (52 developers; one school system), and their authors say so. The Institute presents this as a research-informed model it is testing and refining, the way it stress-tests everything.
